(5) World Bank value-chain report (2021) — only front matter/TOC in the extract; no smallholder market-access percentage visible. (6) IFC Country Private Sector Diagnostic (2020) — front matter and figure list only; agribusiness section text not in extract. (7) FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming Egypt study (2017) — TOC only in extract; sections on cropping patterns and marketing not rendered, so no verifiable figure. The specific missing element is any published percentage, range, or ordinal band for the share of Egyptian smallholder farmers accessing formal markets; the strongest source (World Bank 2024) is directional prose only, and the contract-farming participation figure cited in the indicator census is both sub-national and a different construct, and did not appear in the supplied pages for quote verification. 1.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked all four World Bank Findex 2025 Egypt pages (microdata catalog landing, study description, data dictionary F1, get-microdata) for a rural or agricultural credit statistic — these are metadata and variable listings only; the variable names 'borrowed', 'fin22a', 'urbanicity', 'receive_agriculture' appear but no estimates, and the unit of analysis is the individual adult, not the farmer. 2) Checked the Findex download-data page (worldbank.org) — it describes the availability of rural/urban disaggregation for ~300 indicators but publishes no Egypt value on the page. 3) Checked IFPRI/CGIAR 'An Agricultural Policy Review of Egypt' (T2) — retrieved text is title page, table of contents, acronym list and introduction; PBDAC is named in the acronym list but no credit-access share appears. 4) Checked GIZ Gender Value Chain Assessment (T4) — contents page lists an 'Access to financial credit' section and a sample of 100 farmers in Minya and Beni Suef, but the retrieved text stops before any figure. 5) Checked the Exa publication page on PBDAC/ABE restructuring (T5) — supply-side loan value and credit-covered-area figures only, wrong construct and inadmissible tier for a statistic. Dead ends: no CAPMAS agricultural census page, no Central Bank of Egypt financial-inclusion release, and no FAO/IFAD Egypt rural finance figure was among the supplied pages. Concluding: found=false, ratification hold.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: The evidence does not establish any farmer-denominated percentage at all, so no cut point — not even the lowest, 10 percent — can be shown to be passed or not passed. Specifically, no source in the retrieved set reports the number or proportion of Egyptian agricultural holders who obtained or could obtain formal agricultural credit; the closest quantities are national adult borrowing variables (no values published on these pages) and supply-side loan/area aggregates. The nearest admissible evidence base for Egypt is the Global Findex 2025 (T1, World Bank), whose Egypt file is described in the retrieved metadata as covering individuals ('UNIT OF ANALYSIS Individual', 'GEOGRAPHIC COVERAGE National Coverage', 1001 cases) with variables 'borrowed', 'fin22a Borrowed from a formal bank or similar financial institution' and a rural/urban breakdown flag 'urbanicity'. Even if a rural sub-population figure were extracted from that source, it would measure (a) adults aged 15+ living in rural areas, a population that includes large numbers of non-farmers, and (b) realised borrowing in the past year, not access to agricultural credit. The indicator's name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS, so the Findex series sits on the wrong side of both the population question and the access-vs-use question flagged in the indicator census. Source 9 (an abstract, T5) reports supply-side aggregates for Egypt — total agricultural loans and the area covered by agricultural credit falling from '1.97 billion in 2009/10 acres to 1.07 billion acres in 2019/20' — which is a portfolio/area measure, not a share of farmers, and is in any case not an admissible tier for a statistic.
1.7.defnote: The name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS; Egypt records rural adults aged 15+ (a population that includes non-farmers) and Nigeria records smallholder households, and both measure borrowing/use rather than access.

For the record, the specific missing item is a published rural-disaggregated mobile broadband population-coverage percentage for Egypt from ITU DataHub, NTRA, MCIT or CAPMAS; without it, even level 1 cannot be evidenced, since level 1 would itself be a claim that rural coverage is below 20%, which the sources equally fail to show. 2.5.note: Value comes from ITU's 2025 price-basket collection under the revised (2024 EGTI) methodology; the 5GB data-only basket replaced the earlier 1.5GB/2GB-era definitions, so the series is not continuous with pre-2025 mobile-broadband affordability figures for Egypt. Next level not proposed: Level 5 would require the value to fall below 1% of monthly GNI per capita. Egypt's 2025 data-only 5GB mobile-broadband basket is 1.58%, and the voice-and-data high-consumption 5GB basket is higher still at 1.92%; only the smaller 1GB voice-and-data basket (0.74%) would clear 1%, and that basket is a voice+data low-consumption bundle rather than a mobile broadband price, so it cannot be used to lift this row to level 5. The indicator name 'Mobile broadband price (% GNI pc)' does not fix the basket allowance, the basket type, or whether the denominator is monthly or annual GNI pc. I have taken ITU's live headline data-only mobile-broadband basket (5GB) as the closest match to 'mobile broadband price', because it is data-only (not voice+data) and is the current published series for Egypt. Its denominator is MONTHLY GNI per capita, per ITU convention — if the row were intended as annual GNI pc the figure would be roughly one twelfth of 1.58. Alternative baskets published for Egypt on the same page for 2025: mobile broadband data-and-voice high-consumption (140 min, 20 SMS, 5 GB) = 1.92%; data-and-voice low-consumption (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB) = 0.74%; fixed-broadband 5GB = 2.52%. The 2GB legacy series that the census flags is not present in the retrieved pages, so no 2GB figure could be quoted.

Source 4 is a 2016 approach paper with no results. Source 6 (IFPRI Egypt SSP) lists publications and blogs but no digital-agriculture yield/income impact figure for Egypt. Source 7 (Forsa midline) evaluates an economic inclusion cash/asset programme, not digital agriculture, and its reported results concern livestock ownership. Source 8 (ClinicalTrials.gov registration of the FAS/IMCHN impact evaluation in Upper Egypt) names household income as an outcome but is Withdrawn with enrollment 0 and no results posted, and the intervention is agribusiness support, not digital. Source 9 is the only page carrying yield and income effect sizes for digital information interventions, and it explicitly lists its study geography as fifteen Sub-Saharan Africa, four India, one Cambodia - no Egypt. Dead ends: no page from MALR, the Agricultural Research Center, ITIDA, or a Digital Egypt / smart-farming programme evaluation was supplied, and no evaluation of an Egyptian agri-advisory platform with a yield or income endpoint appears anywhere in the set. Concluded found=false with a ratification hold.
8.12.note: Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set at any rung: the pages retrieved neither confirm the existence of an Egyptian digital-agriculture impact study with a yield or income endpoint (which would support Adopted/Operating) nor constitute a search wide enough to conclude absence (which would support Absent at level 1). Filling quality_evidence with the IFAD CSPE, or scale_evidence with its US$646.3 million portfolio and 41 km of canals, would add two levels on evidence about non-digital rural development, so both fields are left empty. The indicator names documented yield or income impact evidence, understood within a digital-agriculture maturity assessment as impact of digital agricultural services. The best Egypt-specific evidence available in the retrieved pages is the IFAD Independent Office of Evaluation Country Strategy and Programme Evaluation (EC 2025/129/W.P.3 and its slide deck), which reports that IFAD-financed projects contributed to increased household income and improved food security over 2017-2023 across a US$646.3 million portfolio. That is an income outcome, but the interventions evaluated are canal rehabilitation, drip irrigation conversion, farmer field schools, rural finance and social infrastructure - not digital agriculture. Conversely, the RTI meta-analysis in Global Food Security quantifies yield (+6%) and income (+6%) effects of digital information interventions, but its 20 studies are fifteen from Sub-Saharan Africa, four from India and one from Cambodia, so it carries no Egyptian observation and cannot be transferred across the border. The census's own open question - that Egypt's level 3 rests on an evaluation measuring diffusion and adoption of digital tools rather than yield or income - is confirmed by what these pages contain: no Egyptian digital-agriculture evaluation with a yield or income endpoint surfaced.
8.12.defnote: The name's parenthetical fixes the outcome as yield or income, but Egypt's level 3 rests on an evaluation whose measured outcome is diffusion and adoption of digital tools, not yield or income.

8.11.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS microdata/metadata catalog (T1) — checked the GENERAL_PUBLICATIONS collection listing (11 studies, Egypt in Figures and Statistical Yearbooks 2010-2017); no study or variable relating to language of service delivery; dead end. 2) UN DESA EGOVKB Egypt country page (T1) — reviewed EGDI, EPART, Online Service Index, TII and HCI series; the OSI is the nearest sub-index touching online service features, but the country page publishes only the composite value (0.70016 for 2024) with no local-language sub-question disclosed; dead end for the named construct. 3) UN DESA Data Center 2024 EGDI table (T1) — confirms Egypt's rank 95 / 0.6699 but is a cross-country ranking table with no language field; dead end. 4) MCIT press release 'ICT Sector Achievements in 2025' in both English and Arabic (T3) — the most substantive Egyptian government artifact retrieved; enumerates Digital Egypt platform services, users, transactions, apps, exclusive digital services and postal outlets, but contains no statement about local-language availability of services and no share; the existence of the Arabic edition evidences Arabic-language government communication, not a measured localisation rate. 5) GHDx record for Egypt Statistical Yearbook 2023 (T5) — bibliographic stub only, no tables surfaced, and T5 could not carry a statistic in any case. Not available in the supplied pages and would be needed to close this cell: a MALR/Digital Egypt agricultural advisory service inventory disaggregated by interface language, or a UN E-Government Survey questionnaire-level (MSQ) extract showing Egypt's response on local-language service provision.
8.11.note: Next level not proposed: Every level, including level 1, requires a figure (or bounded qualitative finding) about the share of services delivered in local languages. The retrieved pages establish only that Egypt operates a national digital service platform with a growing service count and publishes official communications in Arabic; they do not establish what fraction of agricultural or government digital services is available in local languages, nor any range from which such a fraction could be bounded. The named construct is a percentage share of services available in local languages. The best available evidence in the supplied pages is (a) MCIT's press release on 2025 ICT achievements, which is itself published in both Arabic and English and reports that the Digital Egypt platform offered 210 government digital services to 10.7 million users, and (b) UN DESA's Online Service Index for Egypt (0.70016 in 2024). Both are counts/indices of service availability, not language-of-delivery shares, and neither is agriculture-specific. This sits squarely on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question: no Egyptian publisher supplies a denominator (total services) paired with a numerator (services offered in local languages), so the %-share framing of 8.11 cannot be satisfied from published Egyptian sources. Note also that Egypt's linguistic situation differs from the multilingual case the indicator implicitly targets — Modern Standard Arabic is the official and near-universal national language — which is a further reason the %-share formulation may not be meaningful here, but that is a definitional argument, not published evidence, and cannot be scored.
8.11.defnote: Should 8.11 remain a %-share indicator when no country publishes a denominator for local-language service delivery — and the Nigeria bundle's guidance text is contaminated with Egypt-specific content that must be removed regardless of the ruling?

8.17.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the nine supplied pages in order. (1) FAO WaPOR catalog entry for 'Global outlook on climate services in agriculture' — confirms an Egypt case study exists in the 2024 report but the landing page carries no figure; the report PDF itself was not among the supplied pages. (2) and (3) FAO 'Practical Farmers' Toolkit' and FAO policy-support resource page for the Global Outlook — both returned 404 error pages, dead ends. (4) FAO/WMO agrometeorological services feature — global narrative on the 'last mile' gap, names Cambodia, the Philippines and the Greater Horn of Africa, no Egypt figure. (5) FAO GSARS workshop news for Egypt — agricultural statistics capacity building, unrelated to advisory reach. (6) World Bank PID P180480 — read for a results-framework reach target; the text supplied stops mid-sectoral-context and contains only the PDO wording on early warning services plus poverty and farm-structure statistics, no advisory coverage figure. (7) FAO 'Advancing rural advisory services... in Egypt' policy brief — the most on-topic national document; searched for any extension coverage rate and found only the qualitative 'weakened coverage' formulation, plus demographic and poverty percentages. (8) Sustainability 11(3) 685 — supplies 51.9% but for climate-change knowledge in two governorates, not advisory receipt; logged as context in construct_note rather than as the value. (9) WMO WWIS Egypt — supply-side only, ten cities with EMA forecasts. Conclusion: figure not present in supplied pages; recorded as abstain rather than fabricating a reach percentage.
8.17.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — level withheld rather than proposed. The specific missing item is any published national estimate of the percentage of Egyptian farmers or agricultural households receiving climate/weather advisories; without it even level 1 cannot be evidenced, since level 1 asserts a measured value below 20 rather than an absence of measurement. The indicator names climate advisory REACH — the share of farmers receiving climate/weather advisories. The only percentages in the retrieved pages are: (a) a peer-reviewed study (Sustainability 11(3), 685) reporting that 51.9% of 792 surveyed farmers in two Nile Delta governorates had no knowledge of the climate change phenomenon — that is climate-change awareness among a two-governorate sample, not national receipt of advisories, and it is not the inverse of advisory reach either; and (b) FAO's Egypt rural advisory services policy brief, which describes 'weakened coverage of extension and rural advisory services' qualitatively with no coverage percentage and no climate-specific breakdown. On the census's open question, everything available for Egypt sits on the SUPPLY side (WMO WWIS lists official forecasts for ten Egyptian cities via the Egyptian Meteorological Authority; the World Bank Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project P180480 aims 'to strengthen the nation-wide agriculture information system and early warning services'), i.e. issuance and platform existence, not farmer receipt. FAO's Global Outlook on Climate Services in Agriculture (2024) surveys 36 countries and includes an Egypt case study, but the retrieved page is a catalog landing page and carries no Egypt reach figure in the text supplied.
8.17.defnote: Does the indicator measure farmer receipt of advisories, or supply-side issuance (warnings issued, platforms live), which is all either country publishes?

A1-CAND-IMP.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO GIEWS Country Brief on Egypt (T1): checked for a dependency ratio; it reports cereal import requirements in tonnes (29 million tonnes for 2026/27; wheat 13.5 Mt; maize 15.5 Mt) — volume, not ratio, so rejected under the construct rule. 2) UNdata mirror of FAOSTAT item 21035, the exact named indicator (T1): Egypt appears in the country filter list and 19 three-year windows (2000-2002 through 2018-2020) are available, but the rendered rows in the retrieved text cover only Afghanistan, Africa and Albania; no Egypt row is present, so no verbatim Egypt figure exists to quote. 3) FAOSTAT landing page (T1) and the FAO catalog metadata record for the Suite of Food Security Indicators (T1): both are descriptive/metadata only, carrying no country values. 4) OECD 'Policies for the Future of Farming and Food in Egypt' (T2): qualitative statements on import concentration and undernourishment (9.4% in 2022-24) but no cereal import dependency ratio. 5) CGSpace FAO presentation 'Food security in Egypt' (T2): names the indicator and shows a chart for Egypt, but the extracted text carries only axis labels (0-70), no data point. 6) Heliyon article on Egyptian wheat import dependency (via PMC): abstract-level content on wheat, not the cereal import dependency ratio. 7) Food Systems Dashboard indicator table: blocked by a Vercel security checkpoint, no data returned. Conclusion: the value almost certainly exists in FAOSTAT's Suite of Food Security Indicators for Egypt, but it is not present in any supplied page and must not be reconstructed from memory.
A1-CAND-IMP.note: Correct indicator series identified at T1 (FAOSTAT via UNdata), but the country-specific row for Egypt was not present in the retrieved page text; series shown is a 3-year average, latest window 2018-2020. Next level not proposed: Not applicable — proposed_level is 0 by design for carried candidate indicators, and additionally no verifiable Egypt value was recoverable from the supplied pages. Named construct is a ratio (%) of cereal imports to domestic cereal supply. The Egypt-specific evidence available in the supplied pages is volumetric, not a ratio: FAO GIEWS states 'Cereal import requirements for the 2026/27 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 29 million tonnes, about 30 percent above the average' and wheat import requirements of 13.5 million tonnes, maize 15.5 million tonnes. These are tonnage forecasts, not an import dependency ratio, and cannot be converted into one without domestic supply figures that are not in the supplied pages. The CGIAR/FAO presentation (Source 6) names 'Cereal import dependency ratio (percent) (3-year average)' as a chart title for Egypt but the chart values are not present in the extracted text (only an axis scale 0-70 appears). The OECD Egypt review (Source 5) discusses Egypt's high cereal import concentration on Russia and Ukraine qualitatively without publishing the ratio.

A1-CAND-IRR.src: FAO AQUASTAT, Egypt country tables (AQUASTAT 2005), Table 4 Irrigation and drainage
A1-CAND-IRR.note: Dated reference year (2002); AQUASTAT compilation of national Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation statistics. Rounded to 100% because area equipped for irrigation (3 422 178 ha) is reported as identical to cultivated area (3 422 178 ha) in the same table. Next level not proposed: Not applicable: scoring is suppressed for carried candidate indicators, so proposed_level is withheld at 0 by design rather than by evidentiary shortfall. The AQUASTAT table reports 'Total area equipped for irrigation ... as % of cultivated area', which is exactly the named construct. Note that the same source's Table 1 reports cultivated area for 2002 as 3 422 178 ha, identical to the equipped area, so the ratio is 100%. A later AQUASTAT country profile (2016, Source 7) reports cultivated area of 3 761 000 ha for 2013 but the supplied page text does not carry a corresponding equipped-for-irrigation percentage, so the 2002 figure is the most recent quotable value here.
A1-CAND-IRR.tier_detail: Dated reference year (2002); AQUASTAT compilation of national Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation statistics. Rounded to 100% because area equipped for irrigation (3 422 178 ha) is reported as identical to cultivated area (3 422 178 ha) in the same table.
